raw: CHAPTER V. The Wine-shop
en: [Chapter 5] The Wine-shop

raw: A large cask of wine had been dropped and broken, in the street.
en: A large barrel of wine had been dropped and broken in the street.

raw: The accident had happened in getting it out of a cart; the cask had tumbled out with a run, the hoops had burst, and it lay on the stones just outside the door of the wine-shop, shattered like a walnut-shell.
en: It happened during unloading. The barrel rolled out quickly from the cart. The metal bands burst. It landed on the cobblestones right outside the door of the wine shop, shattered like a walnut shell.

raw: All the people within reach had suspended their business, or their idleness, to run to the spot and drink the wine.
en: Everyone nearby stopped whatever they were doing, or not doing, to run to the spot and drink the wine.

raw: The rough, irregular stones of the street, pointing every way, and designed, one might have thought, expressly to lame all living creatures that approached them, had dammed it into little pools; these were surrounded, each by its own jostling group or crowd, according to its size.
en: The rough, uneven stones of the street, pointing in every direction and seeming designed specifically to cripple anyone walking on them, had dammed the wine into little pools. Each pool was surrounded by a crowding group, depending on its size.

raw: Some men kneeled down, made scoops of their two hands joined, and sipped, or tried to help women, who bent over their shoulders, to sip, before the wine had all run out between their fingers.
en: Some men knelt down, scooped the wine with their hands, and drank, or helped women leaning over their shoulders to drink before the wine could leak through their fingers.

raw: Others, men and women, dipped in the puddles with little mugs of mutilated earthenware, or even with handkerchiefs from women’s heads, which were squeezed dry into infants’ mouths; others made small mud-embankments, to stem the wine as it ran; others, directed by lookers-on up at high windows, darted here and there, to cut off little streams of wine that started away in new directions; others devoted themselves to the sodden and lee-dyed pieces of the cask, licking, and even champing the moister wine-rotted fragments with eager relish.
en: Others dipped into the puddles with chipped clay mugs, or even with scarves taken from women's heads, which they squeezed dry into babies' mouths. Some made small mud walls to block the wine as it flowed, while others, directed by neighbors looking out from high windows, ran around to block small streams of wine branching off in new directions. A few focused on the wine-soaked wood from the broken barrel, licking and even chewing the wet, wine-stained fragments with enjoyment.

raw: There was no drainage to carry off the wine, and not only did it all get taken up, but so much mud got taken up along with it, that there might have been a scavenger in the street, if anybody acquainted with it could have believed in such a miraculous presence.
en: There was no drainage system. So every drop of wine was scooped up. And so much dirt came with it that the street actually looked clean afterward, though nobody who knew the neighborhood would ever expect to see it swept.

raw: A shrill sound of laughter and of amused voices--voices of men, women, and children--resounded in the street while this wine game lasted.
en: Loud laughter and cheerful voices of men, women, and children filled the street while this wine hunt lasted.

raw: There was little roughness in the sport, and much playfulness.
en: There was very little roughness in the play, and plenty of fun.

raw: There was a special companionship in it, an observable inclination on the part of every one to join some other one, which led, especially among the luckier or lighter-hearted, to frolicsome embraces, drinking of healths, shaking of hands, and even joining of hands and dancing, a dozen together.
en: There was a strong sense of community, as everyone wanted to share in the excitement together. The luckier ones broke into happy hugs and toasts. There were handshakes all around. Groups of a dozen people joined hands and danced.

raw: When the wine was gone, and the places where it had been most abundant were raked into a gridiron-pattern by fingers, these demonstrations ceased, as suddenly as they had broken out.
en: When the wine was gone, and the places where it had pooled were scraped clean down to the dirt by eager fingers, the celebration stopped just as suddenly as it had started. The man who had left his saw in the firewood went back to work.

raw: The man who had left his saw sticking in the firewood he was cutting, set it in motion again; the women who had left on a door-step the little pot of hot ashes, at which she had been trying to soften the pain in her own starved fingers and toes, or in those of her child, returned to it; men with bare arms, matted locks, and cadaverous faces, who had emerged into the winter light from cellars, moved away, to descend again; and a gloom gathered on the scene that appeared more natural to it than sunshine.
en: The woman who had left a small pot of hot ashes on a doorstep, trying to warm her own frozen fingers and toes or those of her child, returned to it. Men with bare arms and messy hair walked back down to their rooms. Their faces were pale and ghost-like. They had come up into the winter light from dark cellars, and now they disappeared back into them. A dark gloom settled over the street once more, looking far more natural to the street than sunshine ever did.

raw: The wine was red wine, and had stained the ground of the narrow street in the suburb of Saint Antoine, in Paris, where it was spilled.
en: The wine was red, and it stained the ground of the narrow street in the Paris suburb of Saint Antoine where it had spilled.

raw: It had stained many hands, too, and many faces, and many naked feet, and many wooden shoes.
en: It also stained many hands, faces, bare feet, and wooden shoes.

raw: The hands of the man who sawed the wood, left red marks on the billets; and the forehead of the woman who nursed her baby, was stained with the stain of the old rag she wound about her head again.
en: The woodcutter's hands left red marks on every log he cut. The woman nursing her baby had a stained forehead, left there by the dirty red rag she wrapped back around her head.

raw: Those who had been greedy with the staves of the cask, had acquired a tigerish smear about the mouth; and one tall joker so besmirched, his head more out of a long squalid bag of a nightcap than in it, scrawled upon a wall with his finger dipped in muddy wine-lees--BLOOD.
en: Those who had licked the barrel wood had a wild, tiger-like red smear around their mouths. One tall, messy man with a long, dirty nightcap on his head dipped his finger in the muddy wine dregs and wrote on a wall, BLOOD.

raw: The time was to come, when that wine too would be spilled on the street-stones, and when the stain of it would be red upon many there.
en: The time was coming when a different kind of red wine would be spilled on these street stones, and its stain would be red on many of the people there.

raw: And now that the cloud settled on Saint Antoine, which a momentary gleam had driven from his sacred countenance, the darkness of it was heavy--cold, dirt, sickness, ignorance, and want, were the lords in waiting on the saintly presence--nobles of great power all of them; but, most especially the last.
en: Now that the dark cloud had settled back over Saint Antoine, returning after a brief moment of sunshine, the darkness was incredibly heavy. Cold, dirt, sickness, ignorance, and hunger were the lords who served in this neighborhood—all of them powerful nobles, but hunger most of all.

raw: Samples of a people that had undergone a terrible grinding and regrinding in the mill, and certainly not in the fabulous mill which ground old people young, shivered at every corner, passed in and out at every doorway, looked from every window, fluttered in every vestige of a garment that the wind shook.
en: But poverty ruled most of all. People who had been ground down by life shivered at every corner, walked in and out of doorways, looked from windows, and wore tattered clothes that fluttered in the wind.

raw: The mill which had worked them down, was the mill that grinds young people old; the children had ancient faces and grave voices; and upon them, and upon the grown faces, and ploughed into every furrow of age and coming up afresh, was the sigh, Hunger.
en: The system that ground them down was one that made young people look old. The children had aged faces and serious voices. On every face, carved into every wrinkle of age, was the sign of Hunger.

raw: It was prevalent everywhere.
en: It was everywhere.

raw: Hunger was pushed out of the tall houses, in the wretched clothing that hung upon poles and lines; Hunger was patched into them with straw and rag and wood and paper; Hunger was repeated in every fragment of the small modicum of firewood that the man sawed off; Hunger stared down from the smokeless chimneys, and started up from the filthy street that had no offal, among its refuse, of anything to eat.
en: Hunger hung out of the tall houses in the tattered clothes drying on poles. Hunger was patched into the windows with straw, rags, wood, and paper. Hunger was seen in the tiny scraps of firewood the man sawed. Hunger stared down from the smokeless chimneys. It rose from the filthy streets, where there wasn't even a scrap of discarded food to eat.

raw: Hunger was the inscription on the baker’s shelves, written in every small loaf of his scanty stock of bad bread; at the sausage-shop, in every dead-dog preparation that was offered for sale.
en: Hunger was written on the baker's shelves, in every small, bad loaf left in stock. It was there at the sausage shop too, in the cheap, mystery-meat sausages offered for sale.

raw: Hunger rattled its dry bones among the roasting chestnuts in the turned cylinder; Hunger was shred into atomics in every farthing porringer of husky chips of potato, fried with some reluctant drops of oil.
en: Hunger rattled like dry bones among the roasting chestnuts in the metal cylinders, and Hunger was chopped into tiny pieces in the cheap bowls of potato scraps fried with a few drops of oil.

raw: Its abiding place was in all things fitted to it.
en: Its home was suitable in every way.

raw: A narrow winding street, full of offence and stench, with other narrow winding streets diverging, all peopled by rags and nightcaps, and all smelling of rags and nightcaps, and all visible things with a brooding look upon them that looked ill.
en: The narrow, winding street was full of trash and bad smells. Other narrow streets branched off from it in every direction. All of them were filled with people wearing rags and nightcaps, smelling of poverty, and looking grim.

raw: In the hunted air of the people there was yet some wild-beast thought of the possibility of turning at bay.
en: Yet in the desperate look of the people, there was still a wild, animal-like thought of fighting back.

raw: Depressed and slinking though they were, eyes of fire were not wanting among them; nor compressed lips, white with what they suppressed; nor foreheads knitted into the likeness of the gallows-rope they mused about enduring, or inflicting.
en: Though they looked beaten down, there were still fiery eyes among them, tight lips pressed white from anger, and foreheads wrinkled like the hangman's rope they thought about either escaping or using on their enemies.

raw: The trade signs (and they were almost as many as the shops) were, all, grim illustrations of Want.
en: The shop signs were all grim pictures of need.

raw: The butcher and the porkman painted up, only the leanest scrags of meat; the baker, the coarsest of meagre loaves.
en: The butcher painted only the leanest, poorest cuts of meat on his sign, and the baker showed only the coarsest, smallest loaves.

raw: The people rudely pictured as drinking in the wine-shops, croaked over their scanty measures of thin wine and beer, and were gloweringly confidential together.
en: The crude paintings of people drinking in the wine shops showed them huddling over tiny glasses of sour wine and cheap beer, whispering darkly to one another.

raw: Nothing was represented in a flourishing condition, save tools and weapons; but, the cutler’s knives and axes were sharp and bright, the smith’s hammers were heavy, and the gunmaker’s stock was murderous.
en: Nothing was in good condition except for tools and weapons: the knives and axes in the shop windows were sharp and bright, the blacksmith's hammers were heavy, and the gunmaker's weapons looked deadly.

raw: The crippling stones of the pavement, with their many little reservoirs of mud and water, had no footways, but broke off abruptly at the doors.
en: The uneven cobblestone streets, full of mud and puddles, had no sidewalks, ending abruptly at the doors of the houses.

raw: The kennel, to make amends, ran down the middle of the street--when it ran at all: which was only after heavy rains, and then it ran, by many eccentric fits, into the houses.
en: The open sewer gutter ran down the middle of the street, when it ran at all, which was only after heavy rains, and then it flooded into the houses.

raw: Across the streets, at wide intervals, one clumsy lamp was slung by a rope and pulley; at night, when the lamplighter had let these down, and lighted, and hoisted them again, a feeble grove of dim wicks swung in a sickly manner overhead, as if they were at sea.
en: Across the streets, far apart, single streetlamps were hung by a rope and pulley. At night, the lamplighter made his rounds. He lowered each lamp, lit it, and raised it again. A weak line of dim wicks swung overhead when he was done, looking as if they were on a ship at sea.

raw: Indeed they were at sea, and the ship and crew were in peril of tempest.
en: Indeed, they were at sea, and the ship and crew were in danger of a massive storm.

raw: For, the time was to come, when the gaunt scarecrows of that region should have watched the lamplighter, in their idleness and hunger, so long, as to conceive the idea of improving on his method, and hauling up men by those ropes and pulleys, to flare upon the darkness of their condition.
en: The starving people of this area had watched the lamplighter for so long. One day, they would decide to improve on his method. They would hang men from those very ropes and pulleys, to shine a light, they would say, on their miserable lives.

raw: But, the time was not come yet; and every wind that blew over France shook the rags of the scarecrows in vain, for the birds, fine of song and feather, took no warning.
en: But that time had not come yet; and the winds blowing over France shook the rags of the poor in vain, for the wealthy, beautiful aristocrats took no warning.

raw: The wine-shop was a corner shop, better than most others in its appearance and degree, and the master of the wine-shop had stood outside it, in a yellow waistcoat and green breeches, looking on at the struggle for the lost wine. “It’s not my affair,” said he, with a final shrug of the shoulders. “The people from the market did it.
en: The wine shop was on a corner, looking better than most other shops in the area. The owner stood outside in a yellow vest and green pants, watching the struggle for the spilled wine. "It's not my problem," he said with a shrug. "The market workers dropped it.

raw: Let them bring another.”
en: Let them bring another one."

raw: There, his eyes happening to catch the tall joker writing up his joke, he called to him across the way:
en: Just then, his eyes caught the tall joker writing his graffiti, and he called out to him across the street:

raw: “Say, then, my Gaspard, what do you do there?”
en: "Hey, Gaspard, what are you doing there?"

raw: The fellow pointed to his joke with immense significance, as is often the way with his tribe.
en: The man pointed to his writing with great seriousness, as jokers often do.

raw: It missed its mark, and completely failed, as is often the way with his tribe too.
en: But his joke fell flat, which is also typical.

raw: “What now?
en: "What is this?

raw: Are you a subject for the mad hospital?” said the wine-shop keeper, crossing the road, and obliterating the jest with a handful of mud, picked up for the purpose, and smeared over it. “Why do you write in the public streets?
en: Are you crazy?" said the wine shop owner, crossing the street and wiping out the writing with a handful of mud scooped up from the ground. "Why are you writing on the public street?

raw: Is there--tell me thou--is there no other place to write such words in?”
en: Isn't there, tell me, any other place to write such words?"

raw: In his expostulation he dropped his cleaner hand (perhaps accidentally, perhaps not) upon the joker’s heart.
en: As he argued, he placed his clean hand, perhaps by accident or perhaps on purpose, over the joker’s heart.

raw: The joker rapped it with his own, took a nimble spring upward, and came down in a fantastic dancing attitude, with one of his stained shoes jerked off his foot into his hand, and held out.
en: The joker tapped it with his own hand, jumped high in the air, and landed in a dramatic dance pose, holding one of his dirty shoes which he had pulled off his foot.

raw: A joker of an extremely, not to say wolfishly practical character, he looked, under those circumstances.
en: He looked like an extremely wild, almost wolfish character.

raw: “Put it on, put it on,” said the other. “Call wine, wine; and finish there.” With that advice, he wiped his soiled hand upon the joker’s dress, such as it was--quite deliberately, as having dirtied the hand on his account; and then recrossed the road and entered the wine-shop.
en: "Put it back on, put it back on," said the owner. "Call wine, wine, and leave it at that." With that, he wiped his muddy hand on the joker's tattered clothes. He did it quite deliberately, as if the dirty hand were the joker's fault. Then he crossed the street again and entered his shop.

raw: This wine-shop keeper was a bull-necked, martial-looking man of thirty, and he should have been of a hot temperament, for, although it was a bitter day, he wore no coat, but carried one slung over his shoulder.
en: The wine shop owner was a thick-necked, tough-looking man of thirty. He must have had a hot temper, because even though it was a freezing cold day, he wore no coat, carrying it slung over his shoulder instead.

raw: His shirt-sleeves were rolled up, too, and his brown arms were bare to the elbows.
en: His sleeves were rolled up, leaving his brown arms bare to the elbows.

raw: Neither did he wear anything more on his head than his own crisply-curling short dark hair.
en: He wore nothing on his head, showing only his short, curly dark hair.

raw: He was a dark man altogether, with good eyes and a good bold breadth between them.
en: He was a dark-complexioned man, with good, wide-set eyes.

raw: Good-humoured looking on the whole, but implacable-looking, too; evidently a man of a strong resolution and a set purpose; a man not desirable to be met, rushing down a narrow pass with a gulf on either side, for nothing would turn the man.
en: He looked friendly enough on the whole, but also stubborn and unyielding; clearly a man of strong determination and purpose. He was not someone you would want to meet in a tight spot, because nothing could make him back down.

raw: Madame Defarge, his wife, sat in the shop behind the counter as he came in.
en: His wife, Madame Defarge, sat behind the counter as he walked in.

raw: Madame Defarge was a stout woman of about his own age, with a watchful eye that seldom seemed to look at anything, a large hand heavily ringed, a steady face, strong features, and great composure of manner.
en: She was a stout woman about his age. Her eyes were watchful and rarely seemed to look directly at anything. Her hands were large and covered in heavy rings.

raw: There was a character about Madame Defarge, from which one might have predicated that she did not often make mistakes against herself in any of the reckonings over which she presided.
en: Her face was calm, her features strong, and her composure was total. There was a strength about her that suggested she rarely made mistakes in any of her business calculations.

raw: Madame Defarge being sensitive to cold, was wrapped in fur, and had a quantity of bright shawl twined about her head, though not to the concealment of her large earrings.
en: Being sensitive to the cold, she was wrapped in fur and had a bright shawl wrapped around her head, though her large earrings were still visible.

raw: Her knitting was before her, but she had laid it down to pick her teeth with a toothpick.
en: Her knitting sat in front of her, but she had laid it down to pick her teeth with a toothpick.

raw: Thus engaged, with her right elbow supported by her left hand, Madame Defarge said nothing when her lord came in, but coughed just one grain of cough.
en: In this pose, holding her elbow in her hand, she said nothing when her husband came in, but gave a tiny cough.

raw: This, in combination with the lifting of her darkly defined eyebrows over her toothpick by the breadth of a line, suggested to her husband that he would do well to look round the shop among the customers, for any new customer who had dropped in while he stepped over the way.
en: This, along with a slight raise of her dark eyebrows, signaled to her husband that he should look around at the clients to see if anyone new had arrived while he was outside.

raw: The wine-shop keeper accordingly rolled his eyes about, until they rested upon an elderly gentleman and a young lady, who were seated in a corner.
en: The owner looked around the room until his eyes rested on an older gentleman and a young lady sitting in a corner.

raw: Other company were there: two playing cards, two playing dominoes, three standing by the counter lengthening out a short supply of wine.
en: Other customers were there: two playing cards, two playing dominoes, and three standing by the counter nursing their small drinks.

raw: As he passed behind the counter, he took notice that the elderly gentleman said in a look to the young lady, “This is our man.”
en: As he walked behind the counter, he noticed the older gentleman look at the young lady as if to say, "This is our man."

raw: “What the devil do _you_ do in that galley there?” said Monsieur Defarge to himself; “I don’t know you.”
en: "What on earth are you doing here?" Monsieur Defarge thought to himself. "I don't know you."

raw: But, he feigned not to notice the two strangers, and fell into discourse with the triumvirate of customers who were drinking at the counter.
en: But he pretended not to notice the two strangers, and started talking to the three customers drinking at the counter.

raw: “How goes it, Jacques?” said one of these three to Monsieur Defarge. “Is all the spilt wine swallowed?” “Every drop, Jacques,” answered Monsieur Defarge.
en: "How's it going, Jacques?" one of the three asked Monsieur Defarge. "Is all the spilled wine gone?" "Every drop, Jacques," Defarge replied.

raw: When this interchange of Christian name was effected, Madame Defarge, picking her teeth with her toothpick, coughed another grain of cough, and raised her eyebrows by the breadth of another line.
en: When this exchange of the name "Jacques" was made, Madame Defarge, still picking her teeth, gave another tiny cough and raised her eyebrows slightly higher.

raw: “It is not often,” said the second of the three, addressing Monsieur Defarge, “that many of these miserable beasts know the taste of wine, or of anything but black bread and death.
en: The second customer said to Defarge, "It is not often that many of these poor beasts taste wine, or anything other than hard black bread and death.

raw: Is it not so, Jacques?” “It is so, Jacques,” Monsieur Defarge returned.
en: Isn't that right, Jacques?" "That's right, Jacques," Defarge answered.

raw: At this second interchange of the Christian name, Madame Defarge, still using her toothpick with profound composure, coughed another grain of cough, and raised her eyebrows by the breadth of another line.
en: At this second exchange of the name, Madame Defarge, still picking her teeth calmly, coughed again and raised her eyebrows a bit more.

raw: The last of the three now said his say, as he put down his empty drinking vessel and smacked his lips. “Ah!
en: The last of the three spoke up, putting down his empty glass and smacking his lips. "Ah!

raw: So much the worse!
en: So much the worse!

raw: A bitter taste it is that such poor cattle always have in their mouths, and hard lives they live, Jacques.
en: It's a bitter taste these poor people always have in their mouths, and hard lives they live, Jacques.

raw: Am I right, Jacques?” “You are right, Jacques,” was the response of Monsieur Defarge.
en: Am I right, Jacques?" "You are right, Jacques," Defarge responded.

raw: This third interchange of the Christian name was completed at the moment when Madame Defarge put her toothpick by, kept her eyebrows up, and slightly rustled in her seat.
en: This third exchange of the name was completed just as Madame Defarge put away her toothpick, kept her eyebrows raised, and shifted slightly in her seat.

raw: “Hold then!
en: "Ah, yes!

raw: True!” muttered her husband. “Gentlemen--my wife!”
en: True!" muttered her husband. "Gentlemen, my wife!"

raw: The three customers pulled off their hats to Madame Defarge, with three flourishes.
en: The three customers tipped their hats to Madame Defarge with polite bows.

raw: She acknowledged their homage by bending her head, and giving them a quick look.
en: She acknowledged their greeting with a nod and a quick look.

raw: Then she glanced in a casual manner round the wine-shop, took up her knitting with great apparent calmness and repose of spirit, and became absorbed in it.
en: Then she glanced casually around the shop, picked up her knitting with calm focus, and became absorbed in it.

raw: “Gentlemen,” said her husband, who had kept his bright eye observantly upon her, “good day.
en: "Gentlemen," said her husband, who had been watching her closely, "good day.

raw: The chamber, furnished bachelor-fashion, that you wished to see, and were inquiring for when I stepped out, is on the fifth floor.
en: The simple room you wanted to see, and were asking about when I went out, is on the fifth floor.

raw: The doorway of the staircase gives on the little courtyard close to the left here,” pointing with his hand, “near to the window of my establishment.
en: The entrance to the stairs is in the small courtyard to the left," he pointed. "Right near the window of my shop.

raw: But, now that I remember, one of you has already been there, and can show the way.
en: But now that I think of it, one of you has already been up there and can show the way.

raw: Gentlemen, adieu!”
en: Goodbye, gentlemen!"

raw: They paid for their wine, and left the place.
en: They paid for their wine and left.

raw: The eyes of Monsieur Defarge were studying his wife at her knitting when the elderly gentleman advanced from his corner, and begged the favour of a word.
en: Defarge was watching his wife knit when the older gentleman stepped forward from his corner and asked for a quick word.

raw: “Willingly, sir,” said Monsieur Defarge, and quietly stepped with him to the door.
en: "Of course, sir," Defarge said, walking with him quietly to the door.

raw: Their conference was very short, but very decided.
en: Their conversation was very short but intense.

raw: Almost at the first word, Monsieur Defarge started and became deeply attentive.
en: At the very first word, Defarge startled and listened closely.

raw: It had not lasted a minute, when he nodded and went out.
en: It didn't take a minute before he nodded and walked out.

raw: The gentleman then beckoned to the young lady, and they, too, went out.
en: The gentleman then signaled to the young lady, and they went out too.

raw: Madame Defarge knitted with nimble fingers and steady eyebrows, and saw nothing.
en: Madame Defarge knitted with fast fingers and calm eyebrows, pretending to see nothing.

raw: Mr.
en: Leaving the wine shop, Mr.

raw: Jarvis Lorry and Miss Manette, emerging from the wine-shop thus, joined Monsieur Defarge in the doorway to which he had directed his own company just before.
en: Jarvis Lorry and Miss Manette met Defarge in the doorway he had pointed out to the other men earlier.

raw: It opened from a stinking little black courtyard, and was the general public entrance to a great pile of houses, inhabited by a great number of people.
en: It opened into a dirty, smelly little courtyard and served as the public entrance to a large tenement building home to many people.

raw: In the gloomy tile-paved entry to the gloomy tile-paved staircase, Monsieur Defarge bent down on one knee to the child of his old master, and put her hand to his lips.
en: In the gloomy, tile-paved entryway leading to the gloomy, tile-paved staircase, Monsieur Defarge bent down on one knee before his old master's daughter and kissed her hand.

raw: It was a gentle action, but not at all gently done; a very remarkable transformation had come over him in a few seconds.
en: It was a polite action but done with a tense, serious energy; he had completely changed in just a few seconds.

raw: He had no good-humour in his face, nor any openness of aspect left, but had become a secret, angry, dangerous man.
en: The friendly look was gone from his face, replaced by a secret, angry, and dangerous expression.

raw: “It is very high; it is a little difficult.
en: "It is a long way up, and a bit difficult.

raw: Better to begin slowly.”  Thus, Monsieur Defarge, in a stern voice, to Mr.
en: We should start slowly," Defarge said sternly to Mr.

raw: Lorry, as they began ascending the stairs.
en: Lorry as they began walking up the stairs.

raw: “Is he alone?” the latter whispered.
en: "Is he alone?" Lorry whispered.

raw: “Alone!
en: "Alone!

raw: God help him, who should be with him!” said the other, in the same low voice.
en: God help him, who else would be with him?" Defarge replied in the same quiet tone.

raw: “Is he always alone, then?”
en: "Is he always alone, then?"

raw: “Yes.”
en: "Yes."

raw: “Of his own desire?”
en: "By his own choice?"

raw: “Of his own necessity.
en: "Out of necessity.

raw: As he was, when I first saw him after they found me and demanded to know if I would take him, and, at my peril be discreet--as he was then, so he is now.”
en: He is exactly as he was when I first saw him, after they found me and asked if I would take him in and keep his secret at my own risk. As he was then, he is now."

raw: “He is greatly changed?”
en: "Is he greatly changed?"

raw: “Changed!”
en: "Changed!"

raw: The keeper of the wine-shop stopped to strike the wall with his hand, and mutter a tremendous curse.
en: The wine shop owner stopped, punched the wall with his hand, and swore quietly.

raw: No direct answer could have been half so forcible.
en: No verbal answer could have been half as powerful.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry’s spirits grew heavier and heavier, as he and his two companions ascended higher and higher.
en: Lorry's heart grew heavier as the three of them climbed higher and higher.

raw: Such a staircase, with its accessories, in the older and more crowded parts of Paris, would be bad enough now; but, at that time, it was vile indeed to unaccustomed and unhardened senses.
en: Such a staircase in the old, crowded parts of Paris would be bad enough today, but back then, it was absolutely disgusting to anyone not used to it.

raw: Every little habitation within the great foul nest of one high building--that is to say, the room or rooms within every door that opened on the general staircase--left its own heap of refuse on its own landing, besides flinging other refuse from its own windows.
en: Every small apartment in the building left its garbage right outside its door on the landing, besides throwing other trash out of the windows.

raw: The uncontrollable and hopeless mass of decomposition so engendered, would have polluted the air, even if poverty and deprivation had not loaded it with their intangible impurities; the two bad sources combined made it almost insupportable.
en: The resulting pile of rotting waste polluted the air, and combined with the smell of extreme poverty, it made the building almost unlivable.

raw: Through such an atmosphere, by a steep dark shaft of dirt and poison, the way lay.
en: They had to climb up through this dark, dirty chimney of filth.

raw: Yielding to his own disturbance of mind, and to his young companion’s agitation, which became greater every instant, Mr.
en: Sensing his own growing anxiety and seeing how upset Miss Manette was becoming, Mr.

raw: Jarvis Lorry twice stopped to rest.
en: Lorry stopped twice to rest.

raw: Each of these stoppages was made at a doleful grating, by which any languishing good airs that were left uncorrupted, seemed to escape, and all spoilt and sickly vapours seemed to crawl in.
en: Each time, they stopped near a dirty barred window where any fresh air seemed to escape and bad smells crawled in.

raw: Through the rusted bars, tastes, rather than glimpses, were caught of the jumbled neighbourhood; and nothing within range, nearer or lower than the summits of the two great towers of Notre-Dame, had any promise on it of healthy life or wholesome aspirations.
en: Looking through the rusty bars, they got a sense of the crowded, dirty neighborhood. Nothing they could see held any promise of a healthy or happy life. Nothing, except the distant towers of Notre-Dame Cathedral.

raw: At last, the top of the staircase was gained, and they stopped for the third time.
en: Finally, they reached the top landing and stopped for a third time.

raw: There was yet an upper staircase, of a steeper inclination and of contracted dimensions, to be ascended, before the garret story was reached.
en: There was still a final, steeper, and narrower flight of stairs to climb to reach the attic.

raw: The keeper of the wine-shop, always going a little in advance, and always going on the side which Mr. Lorry took, as though he dreaded to be asked any question by the young lady, turned himself about here, and, carefully feeling in the pockets of the coat he carried over his shoulder, took out a key.
en: Defarge, who had walked slightly ahead on Lorry's side, as if avoiding any questions from the young lady, turned around, reached into the pockets of the coat he carried, and pulled out a key.

raw: “The door is locked then, my friend?” said Mr.
en: "Is the door locked, then?" Mr.

raw: Lorry, surprised.
en: Lorry asked, surprised.

raw: “Ay. Yes,” was the grim reply of Monsieur Defarge.
en: "Yes, it is," Defarge replied grimly.

raw: “You think it necessary to keep the unfortunate gentleman so retired?”
en: "Do you think it necessary to keep the poor man locked away like this?"

raw: “I think it necessary to turn the key.” Monsieur Defarge whispered it closer in his ear, and frowned heavily.
en: "I think it necessary to keep him locked in." Defarge whispered this close to Lorry's ear with a heavy frown.

raw: “Why?”
en: "Why?"

raw: “Why!
en: "Why!

raw: Because he has lived so long, locked up, that he would be frightened--rave--tear himself to pieces--die--come to I know not what harm--if his door was left open.”
en: Because he has lived locked up for so long that he would panic, lose his mind, hurt himself, or even die of fright if the door was left open."

raw: “Is it possible!” exclaimed Mr.
en: "Is that really possible!" Mr.

raw: Lorry.
en: Lorry exclaimed.

raw: “Is it possible!” repeated Defarge, bitterly. “Yes.
en: "Is it possible?" Defarge repeated bitterly.

raw: And a beautiful world we live in, when it _is_ possible, and when many other such things are possible, and not only possible, but done--done, see you!--under that sky there, every day.
en: "Yes. And it's a beautiful world we live in, where such things are not only possible, but actually done to people under the sun every single day.

raw: Long live the Devil.
en: Long live the Devil.

raw: Let us go on.”
en: Let's keep moving."

raw: This dialogue had been held in so very low a whisper, that not a word of it had reached the young lady’s ears.
en: This conversation was held in such low whispers that the young lady didn't hear a word.

raw: But, by this time she trembled under such strong emotion, and her face expressed such deep anxiety, and, above all, such dread and terror, that Mr.
en: But by now, she was trembling with emotion, her face showing such deep worry and fear that Mr.

raw: Lorry felt it incumbent on him to speak a word or two of reassurance.
en: Lorry felt he had to offer some comfort.

raw: “Courage, dear miss!
en: "Courage, dear miss!

raw: Courage!
en: Courage!

raw: Business!
en: Focus on the task!

raw: The worst will be over in a moment; it is but passing the room-door, and the worst is over.
en: The worst will be over in a moment; once we pass the door, the hardest part is done.

raw: Then, all the good you bring to him, all the relief, all the happiness you bring to him, begin.
en: Then, all the help, comfort, and happiness you are bringing to him will begin.

raw: Let our good friend here, assist you on that side.
en: Let our friend here support you on that side.

raw: That’s well, friend Defarge.
en: Thank you, Defarge.

raw: Come, now.
en: Come along now.

raw: Business, business!”
en: Let's do this!"

raw: They went up slowly and softly.
en: They went up slowly and quietly.

raw: The staircase was short, and they were soon at the top.
en: The stairs were short, and they quickly reached the top.

raw: There, as it had an abrupt turn in it, they came all at once in sight of three men, whose heads were bent down close together at the side of a door, and who were intently looking into the room to which the door belonged, through some chinks or holes in the wall.
en: Because the staircase had a sharp turn in it, they suddenly came upon three men standing with their heads close together by a door. They were intently peering into the room through some cracks and holes in the wall.

raw: On hearing footsteps close at hand, these three turned, and rose, and showed themselves to be the three of one name who had been drinking in the wine-shop.
en: Hearing footsteps, they turned around, showing themselves to be the three "Jacques" who had been drinking in the shop downstairs.

raw: “I forgot them in the surprise of your visit,” explained Monsieur Defarge. “Leave us, good boys; we have business here.”
en: "I forgot about them in the excitement of your visit," Defarge explained. "Leave us, guys; we have business here."

raw: The three glided by, and went silently down.
en: The three men slipped past them and went quietly downstairs.

raw: There appearing to be no other door on that floor, and the keeper of the wine-shop going straight to this one when they were left alone, Mr.
en: Since there was no other door on the floor, and the wine shop owner went straight to this one, Mr.

raw: Lorry asked him in a whisper, with a little anger:
en: Lorry asked him in a sharp whisper:

raw: “Do you make a show of Monsieur Manette?”
en: "Are you turning Monsieur Manette into an exhibit?"

raw: “I show him, in the way you have seen, to a chosen few.”
en: "I show him to a chosen few, in the way you just saw."

raw: “Is that well?”
en: "Is that right?"

raw: “_I_ think it is well.”
en: "I think it is."

raw: “Who are the few?
en: "Who are these few?

raw: How do you choose them?”
en: How do you choose them?"

raw: “I choose them as real men, of my name--Jacques is my name--to whom the sight is likely to do good.
en: "I choose men who share my goal, under the name Jacques, for whom this sight will do some good.

raw: Enough; you are English; that is another thing.
en: Anyway, you are English, which is different.

raw: Stay there, if you please, a little moment.”
en: Please wait here for a moment."

raw: With an admonitory gesture to keep them back, he stooped, and looked in through the crevice in the wall.
en: Signaling them to stay back, he leaned down and looked through the crack in the wall.

raw: Soon raising his head again, he struck twice or thrice upon the door--evidently with no other object than to make a noise there.
en: Looking up, he knocked loudly on the door a few times, clearly just to make noise.

raw: With the same intention, he drew the key across it, three or four times, before he put it clumsily into the lock, and turned it as heavily as he could.
en: He then scraped the key across the door three or four times before inserting it loudly into the lock and turning it with as much noise as possible.

raw: The door slowly opened inward under his hand, and he looked into the room and said something.
en: The door slowly opened inward, and he looked in and spoke.

raw: A faint voice answered something.
en: A weak voice answered back.

raw: Little more than a single syllable could have been spoken on either side.
en: They only exchanged a syllable or two.

raw: He looked back over his shoulder, and beckoned them to enter.
en: He looked back over his shoulder and gestured for them to come in.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry got his arm securely round the daughter’s waist, and held her; for he felt that she was sinking.
en: Lorry put his arm securely around the daughter’s waist to support her, feeling that she was about to faint.

raw: “A-a-a-business, business!” he urged, with a moisture that was not of business shining on his cheek. “Come in, come in!”
en: "Remember, focus on the task!" he urged, with a tear running down his cheek that had nothing to do with business. "Come in, come in!"

raw: “I am afraid of it,” she answered, shuddering.
en: "I am afraid of it," she whispered, shivering.

raw: “Of it? What?”
en: "Of what?"

raw: “I mean of him.
en: "I mean of him.

raw: Of my father.”
en: Of my father."

raw: Rendered in a manner desperate, by her state and by the beckoning of their conductor, he drew over his neck the arm that shook upon his shoulder, lifted her a little, and hurried her into the room.
en: Feeling desperate because of her state and Defarge's gestures, Mr. Lorry draped her shaking arm over his shoulder, lifted her slightly, and hurried her into the room.

raw: He sat her down just within the door, and held her, clinging to him.
en: He sat her down just inside the door and held her close as she clung to him.

raw: Defarge drew out the key, closed the door, locked it on the inside, took out the key again, and held it in his hand.
en: Defarge pulled out the key. He closed the door and locked it from the inside.

raw: All this he did, methodically, and with as loud and harsh an accompaniment of noise as he could make.
en: Then he removed the key again and kept it in his hand.

raw: Finally, he walked across the room with a measured tread to where the window was.
en: He did all of this methodically, making as much noise as possible.

raw: He stopped there, and faced round.
en: Finally, he walked slowly across the room to the window, stopped, and turned around to face them.

raw: The garret, built to be a depository for firewood and the like, was dim and dark: for, the window of dormer shape, was in truth a door in the roof, with a little crane over it for the hoisting up of stores from the street: unglazed, and closing up the middle in two pieces, like any other door of French construction.
en: The attic, built as a storage room for firewood, was dim and dark. The window was actually a door in the roof, with a small crane over it to hoist goods from the street. It had no glass and opened in the middle like a double door.

raw: To exclude the cold, one half of this door was fast closed, and the other was opened but a very little way.
en: To keep out the cold, one half of this door was shut tight, and the other was opened only a tiny crack.

raw: Such a scanty portion of light was admitted through these means, that it was difficult, on first coming in, to see anything; and long habit alone could have slowly formed in any one, the ability to do any work requiring nicety in such obscurity.
en: Very little light came through, making it hard to see anything at first; only long habit could give someone the ability to do fine work in such darkness. Yet that kind of work was being done.

raw: Yet, work of that kind was being done in the garret; for, with his back towards the door, and his face towards the window where the keeper of the wine-shop stood looking at him, a white-haired man sat on a low bench, stooping forward and very busy, making shoes.
en: A white-haired man sat on a low bench, leaning forward, busy making shoes. His back was to the door. His face was turned toward the window where Defarge stood watching.
